<!-- section:why -->

A setting or a compositional rule is useful only when it serves your intention. This lesson helps you explain a choice and inspect its consequence.

<!-- section:understand -->

Composition is an intentional arrangement of attention. Subject placement, contrast, scale, and surrounding space can each change what the viewer notices first. Make two frames and ask a viewer what they noticed first before explaining your intent. Their answer gives you a useful comparison.

<!-- section:see -->

Photograph a fictional lone tree once in the center and once near the edge with open space toward distant hills. The centered view may feel formal; the offset view may connect the tree to the landscape. These are interpretation hypotheses, not universal viewer responses.

<!-- section:deeper -->

The rule of thirds is a prompt for alternatives, not a grading rule. Symmetry or a centered subject may better serve the idea.

<!-- section:customer -->

I placed the tree here to connect it with the empty field; we can compare a centered frame to see which communicates the intention.

<!-- section:try -->

A portrait is perfectly aligned to thirds, but a bright sign draws attention away. Name a useful next adjustment.

<!-- section:revisit -->

Reframe, change viewpoint, or wait for different light to reduce the sign’s competition. Grid compliance is less relevant than whether the intended subject reads clearly.
